rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - the authors grew sweet corn in 25 L soil columns in fall 2004 and spring 2006 with three fertilizer residence-time treatments (1, 3, 7 d before a forced leaching event) and measured weekly N uptake, biomass, ear yield, root length density and FUE (Table 1, Fig. 4-7).
rows.notes: The study does not test soil sensors, sensor-based scheduling or any irrigation scheduling practice; irrigation was applied uniformly and columns were kept near field capacity. The experimental factor is the residence time of fertilizer N before an artificial leaching event, which the authors describe only as 'indicative of' better irrigation practices. It shows that longer N retention in the root zone increases growth, ear yield and N uptake (Table 1), but the link to sensor-based or frequent small-volume irrigation is an inference, not a measured result. No crop water stress was imposed or measured.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - own column experiment over two seasons with three N residence-time treatments; potential N leaching was calculated as applied N minus measured plant uptake (Fig. 7).
rows.notes: The study does not evaluate soil sensors or irrigation scheduling. Leaching was forced by applying 2 pore volumes of water at fixed intervals; 'potential N leaching' is a calculated difference between applied N and plant uptake (cumulative 253/223/101 kg N ha-1 in fall and 282/159/85 in spring for tR 1/3/7 d), not a measured response to a scheduling or sensor technology. The result shows that keeping N in the root zone longer reduces the unused N available to leach, which the authors attribute by assumption to better irrigation management; it is not own evidence on sensor-based or high-frequency low-volume irrigation.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a controlled column (lysimeter-type) experiment on fertilizer N residence time in sweet corn on Candler fine sand; it contains no irrigation scheduling or sensor treatment, so both claim rows are technology mismatches.
